name: Claude Code
lede: Anthropic's coding agent in the terminal and IDE: stage 0 of our ladder, today.
what: An agentic coding tool that reads a repository, runs commands and edits files, with permission modes, hooks, MCP connections and subagents. Runs headless with claude -p.
apart: It runs with the engineer's own access and asks before acting, so a human is the gate. Managed settings, project instruction files and hooks encode team conventions and checks once.
stand: In use. Next: managed settings, telemetry on, and hooks that run our policy checks locally. ⚠️ Check flag names against current docs.
src: Anthropic documentation; CLAUDE-AGENT-PLATFORM.md
note: Stage 0 isn't nothing: it's where our engineers learn what the model is good and bad at before any automation exists.

name: Claude API and Amazon Bedrock
lede: The model calls behind every agent we host: direct from Anthropic, or through AWS.
what: The Messages API with tool use, prompt caching, batch processing and structured outputs. The same models are offered through Amazon Bedrock, Google Vertex AI and Microsoft Foundry.
apart: Direct: newest features first. Bedrock: the AWS IAM, billing and private networking we already govern, with IRSA and no static keys; some features arrive later. Prompt caching and batch are the big cost levers on either.
stand: We recommend Bedrock with IRSA, with a gateway in front either way. ⚠️ Check current pricing and feature availability on both first.
src: Anthropic and AWS documentation
note: For triage the context, runbooks and recent deploys, repeats on every alert. That's exactly the shape prompt caching rewards.

name: Claude Agent SDK and Managed Agents
lede: Two ways to get a full agent loop without writing one, differing in who hosts it.
what: The Agent SDK packages the Claude Code harness as a library: built-in tools, hooks, subagents and permissions, running on our infrastructure. Managed Agents is Anthropic-hosted, with the loop and a per-session sandbox on Anthropic's side.
apart: Agent SDK: our pods, our identity, our egress policy, so it can reach inside our network. Managed Agents: nothing to host, but its sandbox isn't inside our network. ⚠️ Check Bedrock availability.
stand: Trial the Agent SDK for agents that run as cluster workloads. Keep Managed Agents for self-contained work only.
src: Anthropic documentation
note: The rule: if the agent's tools live in our clusters, we host the loop.

name: Model Context Protocol
lede: The standard way an agent reaches a tool, and the thing we have to govern.
what: An open protocol for exposing tools and data to models. MCP servers wrap an API or system; clients like Claude Code or our own agents call them.
apart: One integration works across agents and models. The risk is the default: a server inherits whatever credentials the person who started it had. 34 sessions this year were about running MCP safely.
stand: Adopt as the tool interface, with servers run centrally as cluster workloads behind the MCP gateway.
src: MCP track and Agentics Day, KubeCon NA 2026
note: Every MCP server we run should have its own identity and an owner, like any other service.

name: Argo CD MCP server
lede: Lets an agent read real application state instead of guessing.
what: An MCP server exposing Argo CD applications, sync status, health and diffs to an agent.
apart: The first item on ArgoCon's agent-ready checklist. Read-only, it gives triage the deploy context it most needs: what changed, when, and whether it's healthy.
stand: Trial read-only, as one of stage 1's data sources.
src: ArgoCon agent-ready checklist, KubeCon NA 2026
note: ArgoCon's checklist order: integration, progressive delivery, traceability.

name: HolmesGPT
lede: An open-source investigation agent built for alert-driven triage.
what: A CNCF Sandbox project, Apache 2.0: given an alert, the model chooses investigation tools (Kubernetes, Prometheus, logs, 30+ integrations) and follows Markdown runbooks to an explanation.
apart: Agentic and multi-source, unlike k8sgpt's rule-based scan. STCLab cut manual triage from about 20 minutes to under 2 per alert, and found runbook quality mattered more than model choice.
stand: Our stage-1 starting point, read-only, with Claude behind it. ⚠️ Confirm the current release and Claude support.
src: CNCF blog, April 2026; project documentation
note: It pairs naturally with the knowledge-base practice: its runbooks are our runbooks.

name: k8sgpt
lede: A rule-based Kubernetes scanner with model-written explanations.
what: A CNCF Sandbox project that runs analyzers over cluster resources to find problems, then uses a model to explain them in plain language. CLI and operator modes.
apart: Narrower and more predictable than HolmesGPT: Kubernetes only, analyzers first, model second. Many teams run it as a first-pass scanner.
stand: Watch, or use as a cheap first pass alongside HolmesGPT.
src: Project documentation; 2026 comparisons (vendor-affiliated, directional)
note: Good for 'what's wrong in this cluster right now', less good for 'why did this alert fire'.

name: kagent
lede: Agents as Kubernetes resources, not scripts on a laptop.
what: A CNCF project that defines agents, their tools and models as CRDs and runs them as cluster workloads, with MCP tool support. It reached 1.0 with agent-substrate support at the show.
apart: The lowest-commitment way to make an agent a first-class workload with RBAC, namespaces and GitOps. Floor demo: kagent plus Claude tuning Karpenter.
stand: A phase 3 candidate: whether we stay on Jenkins or move execution to a Kubernetes-native controller, decided with 2027's data.
src: kagent Contribfest; "Kagent 1.0 with Agent Substrate", KubeCon NA 2026
note: Our day-one notes had kagent in the top three, and it held up all week. The platform plan deliberately starts on Jenkins and keeps this as the option.

name: Agent substrate
lede: A vocabulary more than a product: the layer under an agent.
what: Solo.io's framing, taken to a keynote with Anthropic and Google: the layer that gives an agent identity, a sandbox, session and state management, and egress control.
apart: It's a checklist plus emerging implementations, not an install. Its value is making us name where each of the four comes from.
stand: Adopt the checklist as our production-readiness bar; decide implementations piece by piece.
src: "Agent Substrate" and "The Harness Is the New Runtime" keynotes, KubeCon NA 2026
note: If we can't fill in all four boxes for an agent, it doesn't go to production.

name: Kata Containers, gVisor, vCluster
lede: Three ways to stop agent-written code sharing a kernel with everything else.
what: Kata: each pod in a lightweight VM. gVisor: a user-space kernel intercepting syscalls. vCluster: a virtual Kubernetes control plane per agent or tenant inside a host cluster.
apart: Kata gives the strongest isolation, and snapshots (Microsoft's 'Groundhog Pod') make start-up acceptable. gVisor is lighter with some compatibility cost. vCluster isolates the API surface, not the kernel.
stand: A hardened pod now: non-root, read-only filesystem, no host mounts. Kata for any agent that executes generated code, from stage 3.
src: "Sandbox Your Agents" keynote; "Groundhog Pod" (Microsoft); vCluster, KubeCon NA 2026
note: Most agents in stages 1 and 2 never execute generated code; they need the hardened pod, not a microVM.

name: SPIFFE / SPIRE
lede: Short-lived, attested identity for every workload, including agents.
what: SPIFFE is the standard for workload identity documents; SPIRE issues and rotates them after attesting the workload. The new SPIFFE Broker API extends identity to Kubernetes objects.
apart: Replaces long-lived service-account tokens and secrets with certificates that expire on their own. Coinbase runs it across 79 production clusters. Our mesh can supply the same identity more cheaply.
stand: Adopt, and start before the agents arrive: mesh identity first, SPIRE where the mesh doesn't reach.
src: "Every Kubernetes Object Deserves an Identity" (Defakto); Coinbase mTLS talk, KubeCon NA 2026
note: The strongest build-it-in message of the week.

name: Cedar and OpenFGA
lede: Answering 'what can this agent actually do?' with a query.
what: Cedar: AWS's open policy language, designed to be analysed, so you can prove what a policy allows. OpenFGA: a CNCF relationship-based authorization engine on Google's Zanzibar model.
apart: Cedar's analysability is the point for MCP: AWS and Stacklok showed proving what an agent's tool permissions allow. OpenFGA fits permissions that follow relationships: teams, ownership, sharing.
stand: Trial Cedar for MCP tool permissions alongside the Obot and ToolHive bake-off.
src: "What Can Your AI Agents Actually Do? Cedar Analysis for MCP Servers" (AWS, Stacklok), KubeCon NA 2026
note: The question to answer in one query: list every tool this agent can call, and with what scope.

name: Obot
lede: An MCP catalog and gateway, with permissions from the directory.
what: An MIT-licensed platform combining an MCP server catalog, hosting on Docker or Kubernetes, an MCP gateway and an LLM gateway. Production installs need Kubernetes and PostgreSQL.
apart: Governance first: one catalog of approved servers, access granted by directory group. Access control is per server and catalog; detailed logging relies on Kubernetes tooling.
stand: In a two-week bake-off against ToolHive. Decide the enforcement point before the product.
src: Our show notes; vendor comparisons (directional)
note: Our notes called it 'AD-managed MCP permissions', which is exactly the problem it targets.

name: ToolHive
lede: MCP servers as isolated, Kubernetes-native workloads.
what: Stacklok's Apache-2.0 platform runs each MCP server in its own container. Its operator bundles a runtime, registry and gateway, and creates a scoped ServiceAccount and RBAC for every MCP server.
apart: Isolation and per-server identity by default, closer to how we run any other service. More operational weight for teams without cluster expertise.
stand: In the bake-off against Obot.
src: Stacklok documentation; "Cedar Analysis for MCP Servers", KubeCon NA 2026
note: If the enforcement point is per-server identity, ToolHive fits; if it's a central catalog and gateway, Obot fits.

name: AI gateway on Gateway API
lede: One place in front of Claude and our MCP tools.
what: A gateway that routes model and tool traffic with auth, per-team quota, cost attribution and audit. Envoy AI Gateway and kgateway build on Gateway API; vendor proxies offer the same as products.
apart: Building on Gateway API makes it the same data plane as the ingress migration. Much of the ecosystem targets self-hosted models, which we don't need; the egress, quota and audit half is what we use.
stand: One of the four components we build. Trial once the Gateway API migration has an owner.
src: "From Proxy to Platform: Building a Multi-Tenant AI Gateway" (Adobe), KubeCon NA 2026
note: For us the gateway's job is egress to Claude and tool access, not load-balancing model servers.

name: Kyverno for AI traffic
lede: Our policy engine, extended to models and tools.
what: Kyverno policies at admission plus Kyverno's authorization integration with Envoy, deciding which workloads may call which models and which MCP tools.
apart: No second policy language for AI: the same engine and CI checks as Path 1. Write policy against the action, so people and agents share rules.
stand: Trial with the AI gateway.
src: "Integrating Envoy AI Gateway and Kyverno Authz" (Nirmata, Nutanix), KubeCon NA 2026
note: No deck was posted for this one; watch the recording when it lands.

name: OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions
lede: Standard span attributes for model and tool calls.
what: OpenTelemetry semantic conventions for generative AI (model, token counts, operation, tool calls), so model traffic lands in the same traces as everything else.
apart: Being standardised now, with Google and Microsoft pushing a joint effort. Using it means our spans won't need rewriting when the standard settles. Claude Code can export OpenTelemetry telemetry.
stand: Adopt for every Claude and MCP call from day one: it's the inventory of what we use AI for. ⚠️ Pin a convention version; some attributes are experimental.
src: "The Race to Standardize AI Observability" (Google, Microsoft), KubeCon NA 2026
note: Turning this on is phase 0's first item.

name: Cost per task
lede: Pricing AI the way Verkada did: per unit of work.
what: Token usage from Claude responses and spans, joined to team and use-case labels, plus OpenCost allocation for the pods that host agents.
apart: A monthly invoice tells us nothing. Cost per alert triaged or per PR merged, next to human cost, is the business case, and the metric for choosing model tier.
stand: Trial alongside stage 1. ⚠️ Model prices change; read them from current pricing, not this card.
src: Verkada; "Clueless About the Cost of AI Model Usage?" (IBM), KubeCon NA 2026
note: Verkada's figure was 33 cents an alert. We want our own number by the end of the stage-1 pilot.

name: Cadence
lede: Durable workflows for agents that act over many steps.
what: An open-source durable workflow engine from Uber: workflow state is persisted, so a multi-step job survives crashes and resumes or compensates cleanly. Temporal is its better-known descendant.
apart: Makes a half-finished multi-step change recoverable instead of leaving infrastructure in an unknown state.
stand: Watch. It becomes relevant at stage 4, when agents take multi-step actions; not before.
src: "Agents Fail, Workflows Recover: Durable Agent Orchestration with Cadence", KubeCon NA 2026
note: If we get there, compare Cadence and Temporal on the operational burden we can staff.

name: Path 1's delivery spine
lede: Argo CD, GitOps Promoter, Argo Rollouts, Kyverno: carded in Path 1's index.
what: The delivery and policy tools every control here depends on: auto-synced GitOps, PR-based promotion, canaries with analysis, policy in CI and at admission.
apart: Every agent-authored change enters through the same path as a human one. That's why stage 2 is gated on Path 1's stage B.
stand: See the Path 1 deck for each tool's card and the promotion decision.
src: Path 1: Deployments as a service
note: If someone asks why the agent deck needs the delivery deck: a change is safe because of how it ships, not who wrote it.
